title: Understanding God through the game of experiences
intro: Uday’s purpose is to make an abstract spiritual idea imaginable: to understand who we are, remember that understanding during life, and recognize the same Creator in others.

sections.title: A story the mind can visualize
paragraphs: Imagine being the one Creator, with the power to create anything, but alone, with nobody else to meet. In Uday’s telling, being alone becomes boredom: what would you experience with all those powers? You create a world of many lives, relationships, and situations, then enter it through its different roles. This is the game of experiences.

The story brings an abstract idea into a scene the mind can picture. The worker, parent, friend, and stranger are roles within the experience; the Creator is the shared identity through them. Having designed the game before entering, we cannot change its complete design from inside. Forgetting, remembrance, effort, learning, and helping are themselves parts of its unfolding.

Uday offers this as a philosophical explanation of creation and identity. The loneliness and boredom express the motive in his account. Readers can examine that explanation and ask whether it makes sense to them. Its purpose is to make understanding accessible and bring remembrance into life.

sections.title: Still God, experiencing life within the rules
paragraphs: In Uday’s teaching, entering this game does not mean that we cease to be God. We are the same Creator who voluntarily entered different lives without the unrestricted powers of the Creator available to each individual role. The limitation belongs to the way the game is experienced; it does not remove our shared divine identity.

Why enter without those powers? Uday explains that, with every power freely available, there would be no need for a body or a car: nothing would need to be reached, learned or experienced through them. To have the experiences of embodied life, the Creator voluntarily enters a game with different rules, needs and limitations. Living through these conditions is the purpose of entry in this account.

Remembering “I am the Creator” therefore means recognizing who is having the experience while continuing to live within the game’s rules. Recognizing this identity does not give the individual unrestricted powers or the ability to rewrite the design from inside. The same divine identity belongs to everyone, not only to the person who understands the teaching.

sections.title: Understanding that carries into life
paragraphs: Knowing the words is a beginning. Understanding means being able to explain their meaning and recognize their relevance in an actual scene. When criticism absorbs you, which role feels threatened? When a plan changes, are you participating or demanding control of the whole game? Can you remember the same Creator in the person before you?

The intended state of mind is remembrance while fully experiencing life. Joy, grief, love, and uncertainty can still arise. The movie illustrates becoming absorbed and then remembering; the lotus illustrates remaining within experience with inward lightness. A feeling does not have to disappear to make enquiry worthwhile.

This understanding is intended to change how we live together. A person’s religion, nationality, wealth, or disagreement cannot remove them from the shared identity described here. Helping, protecting, questioning, and repairing relationships unfold within the game. The teaching invites these responses without promising that one explanation will end every conflict.

sections.title: Why Ashtavakra feels close to this teaching
paragraphs: Uday sees his explanation as a simpler, more concrete way into an insight close to Ashtavakra’s: our identity is deeper than the passing body, mind, and role. The Ashtavakra Gita points toward already-free awareness and the same Self in all beings. Uday’s game story makes shared identity and remembrance easier to visualize.

The connection can be explored without making their explanations identical. Ashtavakra’s timeless Self is beyond change and individual doership. Uday describes creation and entry through a story with a sequence. The Creator’s boredom and the game designed before entry belong to Uday’s explanation; they are not quotations from Ashtavakra.

sections.title: Question beliefs that ask you to harm others
paragraphs: Understanding God must include the person standing before us. If we recognize the same Creator in every life, another person’s religion cannot make their life disposable. A promise of divine reward cannot justify murdering people because of their faith.

Ask what a claim actually says, where it comes from, and whether the promised reward is being used to stop you from questioning harm. A teacher’s certainty, a group’s approval, or a frightening threat is not a substitute for understanding. You can question this website and Uday’s explanation too.

The exploitation of children by terrorist groups is documented. UNODC describes propaganda, deception, coercion, and the exploitation of vulnerability among recruitment methods. Children subjected to such recruitment need protection and support. Claims about a particular institution or country require evidence identifying those responsible.

Challenge harmful teachings and the people or organizations promoting violence. Recognizing the same Creator includes innocent people who share their religion or nationality. Assigning guilt to an entire community repeats the separation this teaching asks us to examine. Protecting someone from harm, setting a boundary, and seeking appropriate lawful help remain participation within the game.

sections.title: Confidence, success, intelligence and oneness
paragraphs: What can this understanding bring into everyday life? Uday presents confidence, success, personal growth, good relationships, intelligence, peace and well-being as the benefits of recognizing our oneness. The invitation is to let the root understanding become a settled way of seeing and living.

“I am the Creator who has come into the game.” In this teaching, this remembrance becomes a state of mind: seeing the world from our shared source while participating fully in work, relationships and ordinary life. Everyone belongs to that same reality.

In Uday’s account, who comes to this website, when they arrive, which pages they read, how often they return, how long understanding takes and how much they gain all belong to the design. He also relates readiness to favorable planetary timing within his spiritual worldview. Encountering the teaching may be understood as arriving when one’s time has come; planetary influence is a belief here, not an established cause of health or success.

Leave the outcome to the design and do the work that is yours to do. Reading, questioning, learning, helping others, seeking care and acting on practical knowledge are themselves part of that design. Difficulty, illness or a slow understanding is not evidence that someone is spiritually inferior or has failed.

These are the benefits Uday associates with his spiritual teaching. Experiences and outcomes vary. Reading or understanding cannot guarantee health, wealth, success or a repaired relationship. Spiritual reflection can accompany appropriate healthcare; it should not replace diagnosis, treatment or prescribed medicine.
links: Explore the benefits and the role of design

reflection: Choose one belief you have repeated without examining. What does it mean, and what supports it? In a real encounter, remember the Creator who designed and entered the game and cannot rewrite its design from inside. Does your understanding include the other person? What response can unfold with that recognition? Leave room for an honest question or for no immediate change.
